t: WA's short-stay rules now carry real penalties
s: WA's first short-stay infringement arrived in August. From registration numbers to planning approvals and renewals, here are five developments worth checking before Perth's summer booking season.
x: WA's short-stay rules now carry real penalties · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents THE RULES · WA SHORT-STAY REGISTER WA's short-stay rules now carry real penalties Last reviewed: 17 November 2026 WA's first short-stay infringement arrived in August. From registration numbers to planning approvals and renewals, here are five developments worth checking before Perth's summer booking season. 4 min read Share What changed Consumer Protection has begun issuing fines, and the 1 January 2026 rules are now in force. Who it affects every hosted and unhosted short-term rental provider in WA. What to do confirm your registration is current and your number is shown in every advertisement. Western Australia's short-stay framework has stopped being a form-filling exercise and started producing penalties, published registers and council decisions. For a host, the practical question each month is narrow: is anything new that I have to act on? Here are the five developments that matter most right now, newest first, each with the one thing to do about it. First infringement, 21 August 2026. Consumer Protection announced its first A$2,000 infringement under the short-stay laws, over an advertisement for a Perth metropolitan home that allegedly did not show a registration number (full story, page 22). Open every live listing and check your number is visible and correct. Anyone can check a listing. The STRA Register's public check tool lets you confirm whether an address is registered or a number is valid. Regulator: Department of Local Government, Industry Regulation and Safety. It covers all WA. Use it to verify a property before you co-host, sublet or buy, and to confirm your own entry reads correctly. Planning compliance under scrutiny. Since 1 January 2026, providers must be able to demonstrate that their properties meet applicable development-approval requirements to remain registered. The obligation to register before advertising has applied since 1 January 2025. Certain offences carry maximum court-imposed fines of A$20,000 for an individual and A$100,000 for a corporation. If you operate unhosted accommodation, check your local planning requirements rather than assuming registration alone is enough. Councils are applying their own local rules. The City of Fremantle's unhosted policy is now live, with its scheme change, Amendment 88, gazetted on 9 January 2026; the City of Mandurah's Amendment 8 is progressing through the Western Australian Planning Commission. These are local-government planning rules that sit on top of state registration, and they differ from council to council. Check your own council's position before you take unhosted bookings beyond the exemption, because a state registration does not settle the planning question on its own. Renewals run on your own date. A registration expires 12 months after it is completed, so every property renews on its own anniversary, not a common date. The register sends reminders as expiry approaches, and renewal costs A$100. A lapsed registration cannot lawfully advertise or take bookings, so make sure the reminder email reaches an inbox someone reads, and renew before the date passes. "Displaying a registration number is not optional." Trish Blake, Commissioner for Consumer Protection. WA rules at a glance Registration has been mandatory for all hosted and unhosted STRA since 1 January 2025. Fees: A$250 initial registration, A$100 yearly renewal (GST status not stated on the official fees page). Your registration number must be displayed in a conspicuous way in every advertisement. Perth metro: unhosted STRA is generally exempt from development approval for up to 90 let nights in the 12-month period counted from registration. Operating beyond that needs planning approval; there is no general statewide 90-night operating cap. t: Register first, list second: your WA compliance guide
s: Western Australia now fines hosts who get the basics wrong. This is the full, practical guide to being legal today: who registers, what it costs, where your number goes, how the 90-night exemption really works, and what ends a registration.
x: Register first, list second: your WA compliance guide · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents LEAD FEATURE · BE LEGAL IN WA Register first, list second: your WA compliance guide Last reviewed: 17 November 2026 Western Australia now fines hosts who get the basics wrong. This is the full, practical guide to being legal today: who registers, what it costs, where your number goes, how the 90-night exemption really works, and what ends a registration. 10 min read Share A well-run Perth short-stay starts with paperwork, not styling: register the property before the first guest arrives. What changed the state has moved to enforcement, issuing its first fine in August 2026. Who it affects every hosted and unhosted STRA provider in WA, including tenants and strata owners. What to do register, display your number in every advertisement, and stay inside your planning limits. The fine that made it real In August 2026 a provider letting a home in the Perth metropolitan area became the first to receive an infringement under Western Australia's short-stay laws. The amount was A$2,000. The allegation was not about noise, parties or tax. It was that the advertisement did not show a registration number (the case is on page 22). Announcing it, the Commissioner for Consumer Protection, Trish Blake, put it plainly: "Displaying a registration number is not optional." A missing number is easy to fix. Planning approval, strata restrictions and rental permissions can take considerably longer. The safest approach is to work through the requirements in order, starting with registration and ending with the conditions specific to your property. Keys change hands at check-in, but compliance begins with the advertisement, long before a guest arrives. Who has to register Registration has been mandatory for all short-term rental accommodation in WA since 1 January 2025. It does not matter whether you let the whole house or a single room, whether you use Airbnb or take direct bookings, or whether you own or rent. Registration generally applies to residential premises offered to paying guests for short stays; the register's guidance describes premises rented out "for periods of less than 3 months". Some accommodation categories are treated differently, so check the official definition if your property or bookings are unusual. The law splits stays into two kinds. Hosted means the host lives on the property during the stay. Unhosted means guests have exclusive use of the whole dwelling. Both must register. The difference matters for planning, not for registration. Tenants can be caught too. If you rent your home and want to let it short-term, the register's guidance is cautious but clear: it is allowed only "If you are a Tenant in a property and your Residential Tenancy agreement does not prohibit STRA," and it recommends you "discuss the sub-letting arrangement with your landlord or property manager." You would still have to register the premises yourself. Granny flats follow the same logic. A granny flat can be hosted where the host lives in the main house, and the reverse also works: the host lives in the granny flat and lets the main house. If both dwellings on a lot are let, they are treated as unhosted and each must be registered separately. The registration number belongs in every listing, in a place a guest, and an inspector, can plainly see. How to register, and what it costs You register through the WA Government's STRA Register, which runs on a MyAccount login, as either an individual user or a business user if you register on someone else's behalf. You provide the property details the Act requires, confirm whether the accommodation is hosted or unhosted, and pay the fee. As part of registration, demonstration of planning approval may be required, so have your planning position clear before you start. The initial fee is A$250. Registration then has to be renewed every year, and the renewal fee is A$100. The official fees page

t: What 5,438 recently reviewed Perth listings reveal
s: A Western Host analysis of public Airbnb listing data for the 30 Perth metropolitan councils: how many listings were recently reviewed, how many are whole homes, what they ask per night, and where they are.
x: What 5,438 recently reviewed Perth listings reveal · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents PERTH BY THE NUMBERS What 5,438 recently reviewed Perth listings reveal Last reviewed: 18 November 2026 A Western Host analysis of public Airbnb listing data for the 30 Perth metropolitan councils: how many listings were recently reviewed, how many are whole homes, what they ask per night, and where they are. 2 min read Share 5,438 Airbnb listings in the Perth metropolitan region with at least one review in the 12 months before the data was collected on 22–23 September 2026 (out of 6,268 listed). 76% share of those recently reviewed listings that are entire homes or apartments. A$296 median advertised nightly price, from 5,071 recently reviewed listings with a usable price (A$350 for entire homes, from 3,845 listings). Top five councils by recently reviewed listings Stirling 762 · Fremantle 544 · Perth 525 · Joondalup 333 · Canning 271 Within the recently reviewed Airbnb listings analysed, the largest counts were recorded in Stirling, Fremantle and the City of Perth. Of the 5,438 Airbnb listings in the Perth metropolitan region that received at least one review in the year before the data was collected in late September 2026, the City of Stirling had 762, followed by Fremantle (544), the City of Perth (525), Joondalup (333) and Canning (271). Three in four of these listings were entire homes or apartments. Under WA planning rules, unhosted short-stay accommodation in metropolitan Perth generally requires development approval when operated beyond the 90-night exemption (see page 6). An Airbnb listing classified as an entire home is not necessarily unhosted under WA law; its actual circumstances determine the applicable requirements. The median advertised price was A$296 a night, calculated from 5,071 listings with usable prices, and A$350 for entire homes (3,845 listings). These are the nightly prices Airbnb quoted for near-term stays, not what guests actually paid, and the data does not say whether they include GST. One quoted price above A$10,000 a night was excluded as an extreme outlier. The figures cover Airbnb listings only, not other platforms, and they are not a count of registered properties. A current official WA register total was not available to us. Key point: Three in four recently reviewed Airbnb listings were entire homes or apartments. That does not establish how many are legally classified as unhosted accommodation. t: Platforms now report your short-stay income to the ATO
s: Since July 2023, booking platforms have given the ATO regular information about short-stay transactions. Here is what owners must declare, what may be deductible, what changed for holiday homes in 2026, and why records matter.
x: Platforms now report your short-stay income to the ATO · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents MONEY · TAX AND REPORTING Platforms now report your short-stay income to the ATO Last reviewed: 17 November 2026 Since July 2023, booking platforms have given the ATO regular information about short-stay transactions. Here is what owners must declare, what may be deductible, what changed for holiday homes in 2026, and why records matter. 9 min read Share Good tax outcomes start with ordinary record-keeping: platform statements, receipts and a simple log of nights rented. What changed Covered booking platforms report short-stay transactions to the ATO twice a year, and in May 2026 the ATO issued new guidance on rental deductions and holiday homes. Who it affects Property owners and tenant-operators earning short-stay accommodation income, and co-hosts or property managers receiving fees for their services. Their reporting and tax treatment may differ. What to do Reconcile gross rental income, calculate allowable deductions carefully, keep adequate records and seek registered tax advice when needed. The quiet part of running a short stay is the paperwork. A host who lists a Scarborough apartment on two platforms, takes a few direct bookings and keeps the odd forfeited deposit is now covered by a more systematic reporting framework, while older ATO data-matching programs show that accommodation income has been under scrutiny for years. The money still arrives the same way. What has changed is how much the ATO already knows. For a Perth operator heading into peak season, the sensible response is not worry: it is good records and an honest return. The platforms report twice a year The mechanism is the Sharing Economy Reporting Regime. Since 1 July 2023, operators of covered booking platforms have had to report short-term accommodation transactions to the ATO. Transactions from 1 July to 31 December are reported by 31 January, and transactions from 1 January to 30 June by 31 July. That sits on top of earlier work. One ATO data-matching program estimated it would collect records about up to 190,000 individuals from accommodation platforms for the 2016–17 to 2019–20 years, including fields such as date of birth and nights booked. The ATO can use this information for compliance and data matching, but platform income may not automatically appear in a taxpayer's return. Owners remain responsible for reporting their income accurately. Owners and managers report different income. An owner generally reports gross rental income, before platform commissions and property-management fees are deducted. A manager or co-host generally accounts for their own service income under the rules that apply to their business. Money collected for an owner is not automatically the manager's income; the correct treatment depends on the arrangement and whose income the payment is. Expenses must be split between private and guest use on a fair and reasonable basis, which is easier when the records are ready before you start. Declare everything, not just the rent Leaving income out is on the ATO's list of common mistakes. You must declare all the income you receive from renting out a property, and the ATO's list expressly includes short-term rentals and renting through a sharing platform. It does not stop at the nightly tariff. Bond or deposit money you keep in place of rent or because of damage counts as income, and so can insurance payouts for lost rent. Where a property is co-owned, rental income is generally divided according to the owners' legal interests, subject to limited exceptions. How deductible expenses are shared also depends on the ownership interests and the nature of the costs. Deductions: only the income-earning share The ATO requires expenses to be apportioned on a fair and reasonable basis when a property, or part of it, is used for more than one purpose or rented for only part of the year. t: A 25-point check before Perth's peak season
s: Perth's busiest short-stay months run from December to February, on hot days, full pools and a live bushfire season. This one-page audit sorts the legal requirements from good practice, with the WA source for each.
x: A 25-point check before Perth's peak season · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents PRACTICAL TOOLKIT · SUMMER READY A 25-point check before Perth's peak season Last reviewed: 17 November 2026 Perth's busiest short-stay months run from December to February, on hot days, full pools and a live bushfire season. This one-page audit sorts the legal requirements from good practice, with the WA source for each. 7 min read Share What to check 25 items across safety, guest comfort, your listing and your neighbours, before the summer rush. Who it affects Every WA host, owner, co-host and property manager running a residential short stay. What to do Work the list once now, fix anything marked Law first, and keep the sheet with your property file. As the summer holidays approach, short-stay operators face tighter turnarounds and less room for a forgotten detail. A dead smoke alarm battery, a pool gate that no longer self-latches, or a listing missing its registration number are the kind of small gaps that are cheap to fix in November and expensive to discover in January. This audit is built to be printed on one page and worked through room by room. It separates two very different things. Some items are the law in Western Australia, and the obligation is usually triggered the moment a dwelling is rented or made available for hire, which is the category that captures short-stay letting. Others are good practice: not legally required of a short stay as such, but the difference between a smooth season and a bad review or a worse incident. Where an item is marked Law , we name the WA regulator and the page it comes from, all read on 17 November 2026. Where the law is genuinely unclear for short stays, we say so and treat the item as good practice. None of this replaces advice from the regulator or your local government, and the detailed technical rules (exact fence heights, alarm placement, ventilation openings) sit in the regulators' own guides. Start with the items marked Law, then work the rest. One habit worth keeping: date and sign the sheet each time. A dated check records what you inspected and what work is still outstanding. The 25-point audit Legend: Law = a legal requirement in Western Australia (triggered on rent or hire). Law where applicable = required for some properties only, as explained. Good practice = recommended, not a short-stay-specific legal requirement. Law · B&E-RCD ☐ 5 Electrical and gas work done by appropriately licensed people where legally required Do not undertake regulated installation, repair or modification work without the right licence. t: Airbnb restricts checkout chores: what hosts need to know
s: For bookings made from 20 November 2026, Airbnb's new policy generally prohibits demanding substantial checkout chores, including stripping beds and washing dishes. Here is what remains acceptable and how hosts can prepare.
x: Airbnb restricts checkout chores: what hosts need to know · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents THE PLATFORMS · AIRBNB HOUSE RULES Airbnb restricts checkout chores: what hosts need to know Last reviewed: 18 November 2026 For bookings made from 20 November 2026, Airbnb's new policy generally prohibits demanding substantial checkout chores, including stripping beds and washing dishes. Here is what remains acceptable and how hosts can prepare. 4 min read Share For Airbnb bookings from 20 November, guests can no longer be required to do the washing-up. What changed Airbnb's new House Rules policy applies to reservations booked on or after 20 November 2026. Who it affects hosts and co-hosts with Airbnb listings. What to do review your House Rules, remove any checkout chores that no longer comply, and check your turnover arrangements. On 20 October 2026 Airbnb told hosts it was changing what they may ask of guests at checkout. The policy is published on Airbnb's Australian Help Centre and applies to reservations booked from 20 November 2026. What guests can no longer be asked to do. Airbnb says hosts generally cannot require tasks that take significant time or effort, or that "would typically be performed by a cleaner". Its examples include washing and putting away dishes, removing sheets or starting a load of laundry, taking rubbish off-site, and avoiding the use of an amenity the listing offers. Airbnb may allow exceptions where a listing's circumstances or relevant local requirements justify a particular rule. What you can still ask. Airbnb lists simple requests that remain acceptable: putting used dishes in the sink, gathering used towels, sorting rubbish and recycling into the indoor bins, and turning off the air conditioning when leaving. Rules must be reasonable and set out in the listing's House Rules section before booking. How Airbnb will enforce it. Airbnb says it will begin reviewing listings on 20 November, with reviews running through March 2027 and continuing after that. It will notify hosts by email and in the app if their rules need attention. Affected hosts will have at least 20 days to update the rules or appeal, and one appeal is allowed. If a rule remains after an unsuccessful appeal, Airbnb may display a notice on the listing and take further action, including reduced search visibility. Hosts generally cannot impose their own fines or penalties for House Rule breaches, although Airbnb permits disclosure of certain fines imposed by local authorities or community associations. What now lands on the host. From 20 November, a guest who books can leave without stripping a bed, washing a cup or taking a bag of rubbish out. Those jobs do not disappear. Depending on what guests leave behind, the host or turnover team may need to strip used beds, remove pillowcases, wash, dry and put away dishes, glasses and pans, empty bins and remove rubbish, alongside the usual cleaning, bed-making and restocking. With back-to-back bookings, all of it has to fit between one guest's checkout and the next guest's check-in, and in a busy summer that can happen several times a week. Whether you do your own turnovers or use a cleaner, hosts should ensure these tasks are covered in their turnover arrangements where needed, allowing enough time before the next arrival. Separate contracts are restricted. Airbnb permits them only in limited circumstances, including certain legal or insurance requirements, community-association rules, monthly-stay rental agreements, Airbnb Luxe listings and agreements covering some optional amenities. Where permitted, contracts must be uploaded through Airbnb's listing settings. Airbnb says it does not require guests to sign them or help enforce them. What this means for WA hosts Bottom line: for bookings from 20 November, substantial checkout chores can no longer be required of Airbnb guests. Who it applies to: Airbnb hosts and co-hosts. t: Renting, granny flats and the 90-night rule
s:
Three common short-stay registration questions, answered using the WA Government's official guidance. This month: operating from a rental, counting the Perth 90-night exemption, and registering a granny flat.

_These questions are adapted from topics in the WA STRA Register's official FAQ; they are not submissions from individual readers. Send us yours for next month._
x: Renting, granny flats and the 90-night rule · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents ASK WESTERN HOST · THE REGISTER Renting, granny flats and the 90-night rule Last reviewed: 17 November 2026 Three common short-stay registration questions, answered using the WA Government's official guidance. This month: operating from a rental, counting the Perth 90-night exemption, and registering a granny flat. _These questions are adapted from topics in the WA STRA Register's official FAQ; they are not submissions from individual readers. Send us yours for next month._ 3 min read Share Tenants can run a short-stay only if the lease allows it and the owner agrees, then the operator registers the premises. I rent the property. Can I register and run a short-stay from it? Possibly. The register's guidance is that a tenant may be able to offer the property, or part of it, as a short stay where the tenancy agreement does not prohibit it, as a subletting arrangement. Check your tenancy agreement and obtain any consent required for the subletting; the register advises tenants to discuss the arrangement with their landlord or property manager. If you go ahead, you as the operator register the premises. Registration is a separate requirement and does not override the conditions of your tenancy agreement, so get the paperwork right before you list. Full text: wa.gov.au STRA register FAQ. When does my 12 months start for the 90 nights? From your registration date, not 1 January. The Perth-metro exemption lets an unhosted property run without development approval where it is "leased for 90 nights or less (non-consecutive) within a 12-month period, as per the date of registration." So if you registered in March, your 90-night year runs March to March. Two things make the counting fairer than it first looks. Only nights actually let to guests count: the register "will capture the number of nights a registered premises is booked," and "Periods when the property is blocked out by an owner for private use are not counted towards nights booked." The register monitors reported bookings and sends notifications at 80 and 90 nights booked. Keep your own accurate records too, including direct bookings, which must be entered manually. Your registration itself also expires 12 months after it is completed, so the renewal and the exemption year run together. Above 90 let nights, you need development approval. Full text: wa.gov.au STRA register FAQ. Do I need to register a granny flat, or a room in my own home? Yes, if you are letting it short-term. The register is clear that "It is now mandatory for all STRA to be registered," whether it is a whole house, a granny flat or a room. What changes is the category. A room you let while living on site is hosted STRA, which is exempt from planning approval across WA but still has to be registered. A granny flat may qualify as hosted where the host lives in the main house, and the reverse can also qualify, where the host lives in the granny flat and lets the main house. If both dwellings are used for short stays, the register treats them as unhosted and each must be registered separately. Register each one you let, and keep each registration number on its own listing. Full text: wa.gov.au STRA register FAQ. "It is now mandatory for all STRA to be registered." x: The missing number behind WA's first fine · Western Host Skip to content ← Issue 1 · December 2026 contents CASE FILE · THE FIRST FINE The missing number behind WA's first fine Last reviewed: 17 November 2026 In August, Consumer Protection announced its first A$2,000 infringement under WA's short-stay laws. The allegation concerned a missing registration number. We look at what the public record confirms, what it does not, and the checks every advertiser can make. 3 min read Share Registration number The case turned on one missing field: the registration number that must appear in every advertisement. What happened a provider was issued a A$2,000 infringement for allegedly advertising a property without its registration number. Who it affects anyone advertising STRA in WA, on any platform. What to do show the correct registration number, conspicuously, in every advertisement. What Consumer Protection confirmed On 21 August 2026 the WA Government announced the first infringement under the state's short-stay laws: A$2,000, issued by Consumer Protection to a short-stay provider. It related to a residential property in the Perth metropolitan area that was allegedly advertised without its STRA registration number. The Commissioner for Consumer Protection, Trish Blake, said the case "demonstrates that Consumer Protection is actively enforcing legislation", and that the agency would keep monitoring compliance. What the announcement did not establish The announcement did not name the provider, the suburb or the platform, and neither do we. It reported that an infringement notice was issued; it did not report whether the notice was paid, challenged or decided by a court. What it shows is the regulator's priority, not a court's finding. Which advertising obligations apply Every advertisement for a registered short stay must show the correct registration number in a readily visible way. Booking platforms and advertising publishers carry their own obligations under the regime, including restrictions on publishing advertisements for unregistered premises and advertisements with a missing or falsely displayed number. Depending on the circumstances, a non-compliant advertisement can expose both the provider and the publisher to regulatory consequences. Certain offences under the STRA legislation carry maximum court-imposed fines of A$20,000 for individuals and A$100,000 for corporations. These are statutory ceilings, not the amount of the infringement notice issued in this case. What a host or property manager can check this week Every live listing (Airbnb, Booking.com, Stayz, your own website, social posts) shows the registration number where a reader can see it. The number is the correct one for that exact property, not copied from another listing. Listings still show it after any platform redesign or listing edit. The public STRA Register confirms the property is registered and the number is valid. That confirms registration only; planning approval and other requirements still need checking separately. The reported A$2,000 infringement is a reminder that a small advertising omission can carry a significant regulatory consequence. "This first infringement demonstrates that Consumer Protection is actively enforcing legislation." Trish Blake, Commissioner for Consumer Protection. The case at a glance The infringement: A$2,000 notice announced by Consumer Protection on 21 August 2026. The allegation: an advertisement for a Perth metropolitan property did not display its registration number. Not reported: the provider's identity, the platform, or any later outcome. The rule: the correct number, readily visible, in every advertisement. The ceiling: maximum court-imposed fines for certain offences of A$20,000 (individual) and A$100,000 (corporation), not the infringement amount.
